title: Was Peter's vision about Gentiles, not food?
summary: Peter himself says the vision was about people: “God has shown me that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Acts 10:28). That concession is real — and it does not revive the kosher code, because Jesus had already declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19) and the Council of Jerusalem imposed no kosher law on Gentiles.
objection: Read Acts 10 for yourself. Peter sees a sheet of unclean animals, refuses to eat, and then explains the vision himself: “God has shown me that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Acts 10:28). He never says the food laws are abolished, never eats an unclean animal, and when he defends himself in Acts 11 he talks only about Gentiles. The vision is about people, not pork. Christians who wave Acts 10 at the dinner table are misreading their own Bible — the dietary laws still stand.

response.heading: Concede the first half: Peter says it is about people.
response.body:
Peter's own interpretation is the text's interpretation — do not fight it. After the sheet descends three times and the voice says, “What God has purified, you shall not call common” (Acts 10:15), Peter goes to Cornelius's house and explains himself: “God has shown me that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Acts 10:28). When challenged in Jerusalem, he retells the whole story and the church concludes, “So has God also given to the Gentiles repentance unto life” (Acts 11:18). The vision's main point, by the author's own telling, is the admission of the Gentiles.

Notice what Peter does not do in the vision: he does not eat. Three times he refuses — “Far be it from me, lord. For I have never eaten anything common or unclean” (Acts 10:14) — and the sheet is taken up uneaten. Anyone who claims Acts 10 shows Peter tucking into pork is inventing a scene the text never stages. The vision is a sign, not a meal, and its stated lesson is about people.

So the objection's first half is right, and a Catholic answer should say so plainly. The question is only whether that first half carries the second half with it: does “the vision is about people” entail “the food laws still bind”? It does not — and the rest of the New Testament is why.

response.heading: The sign is food — and the food question was already settled.
response.body:
Jesus settled the food question before Acts 10 ever happened. “Whatever goes into a man from outside cannot defile him,” He taught, and Mark adds the Church's reading in the text itself: “(Thus he declared all foods clean.)” The Catechism puts it the same way: “Jesus perfects the dietary law, so important in Jewish daily life, by revealing its pedagogical meaning through a divine interpretation” (CCC 582). The dietary laws were a pedagogy — a tutor marking Israel apart — not a moral law written on every conscience forever.

That is why the vision's imagery works at all. God teaches Peter about people by using the food categories Peter already thinks in: the sheet holds “all four-footed beasts, and the crawling things of the earth and the flying things of the air” (Acts 10:12), and the voice commands, “Rise up, Peter! Kill and eat” (Acts 10:13). A sign that meant nothing about food could hardly teach by means of food. The vision does not need to be a food-law repeal to be consistent with one: it presupposes the same movement Jesus had already made, from outward defilement to the heart.

Paul says the same thing without any vision at all: “I know, with confidence in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean in and of itself” (Romans 14:14), and “every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4). Acts 10 is not the load-bearing beam of the Catholic case on food. Mark 7 is. Acts 10 is the illustration of what that teaching looks like when it meets a real Gentile's front door.

response.heading: The Council of Jerusalem imposed no kosher code.
response.body:
If the food laws still bound Gentile Christians, Acts 15 is where the Church would have said so — and she said the opposite. Peter himself stands up and asks why anyone would “impose a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear” (Acts 15:10), concluding, “by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, we believe in order to be saved, in the same manner also as them” (Acts 15:11). The Council's decree then lists four abstentions — “things immolated to idols, and from blood, and from what has been suffocated, and from fornication” (Acts 15:29) — not Leviticus 11. A short pastoral list for Jewish-Gentile table fellowship is not a kosher code.

Paul generalizes the principle: “let no one judge you as concerns food or drink, or a particular feast day, or feast days of new moons, or of Sabbaths. For these are a shadow of the future, but the body is of Christ” (Colossians 2:16-17). The food laws were a shadow; Christ is the body that casts it. To reimpose the shadow after the body has come is to read the Old Covenant as if the New had never arrived — the very mistake the Council of Jerusalem was convened to correct.

None of this means the Church treats food as morally indifferent in every respect. She keeps her own disciplines — Friday abstinence, Lenten fasting — but those are her disciplines, imposed by her own authority for penance and formation, not Leviticus reimposed. The distinction matters: a Church discipline can be changed by the Church; a divine dietary code could not. The Church has never taught that Christians must keep kosher, in any century.

response.heading: What the Church teaches — and what she does not claim.
response.body:
The honest Catholic claim is narrower than the objection pretends, and stronger for it. The Church does not teach that Acts 10, standing alone, abolished the food laws. She teaches that the Law is fulfilled in Christ (CCC 577): its moral core endures, its ceremonial and dietary pedagogy reached its term in Him, and the dietary law in particular was perfected by His divine interpretation (CCC 582). Acts 10 is one scene in that larger story — the scene where Peter learns, by a food sign, that the Gentiles are not unclean.

That reading also respects the one fair point buried in the objection: the Torah never called Gentiles unclean in themselves. The barrier was separation, not Gentile impurity — which is exactly why a food-separation sign was the fitting way to break it. God did not change His mind about pork in order to change His mind about Cornelius; He used the sign of the end of separation to announce the end of separation. “Within every nation, whoever fears him and works justice is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:35).

So grant Peter his interpretation, word for word. The vision is about people. And because it is about people in a Church whose Lord had already declared all foods clean, whose Council refused to yoke Gentiles with the Law, and whose apostle wrote that no food is unclean in itself — the vision's people-lesson and the Church's food-teaching stand together. The objection wins the first sentence and loses the argument.

simple: Some people say Peter's vision in Acts 10 was only about people, not food — and they're half right. Peter himself says God showed him not to call any person unclean. But that doesn't bring back the kosher food rules, because Jesus had already declared all foods clean, and the Council of Jerusalem never told Gentile Christians to keep kosher. The vision used food as a picture to teach Peter about people.
oneLiner: Peter's vision is about people — and that is no problem, because Jesus had already declared all foods clean and the Council of Jerusalem imposed no kosher law.

title: Why can't Catholics and Anglicans share Communion?
summary: Anglicans are baptized brothers in imperfect communion with the Catholic Church (CCC 838) — but Pope Leo XIII judged Anglican orders “absolutely null and utterly void” (Apostolicae Curae, 1896), so without a valid priesthood there is no valid Eucharist to share. The Personal Ordinariates are the open door home.
objection: Anglicans have bishops, priests, altars, and a beautiful liturgy — and Rome accepts their baptisms as valid. Many Anglican clergy trace their succession back through bishops ordained before the break with Rome. So why does the Catholic Church insist their priests are not really priests, their Eucharist is not really the Eucharist, and Catholics may not receive Communion at an Anglican service? The Orthodox kept valid sacraments after their schism, so this looks like favoritism — or just Rome refusing to admit another church is equally a church.

response.heading: Start where we agree: Anglican baptism is real, and Anglicans are brothers.
response.body:
The dispute is not about whether Anglicans are Christians — it is about orders, and only orders. An Anglican baptism performed with water and the Trinitarian formula — “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” — is accepted as valid, and an Anglican entering the Catholic Church is not re-baptized. Baptism is the foundation of communion among all Christians, and the Church receives the baptized with “respect and affection as brothers” (CCC 818).

That is why the Catechism speaks of imperfect communion, not of strangers. Those “who believe in Christ and have been properly baptized are put in a certain, although imperfect, communion with the Catholic Church” (CCC 838). The wound is real — full communion under the successor of Peter is missing — but so is the bond. Nothing in this card is a judgment on the faith, holiness, or sincerity of Anglican clergy or people.

The question, then, is narrow and precise: did the power to ordain priests survive the English Reformation? The Catholic answer turns on what happened to the ordination rite itself in the sixteenth century — not on Anglican piety, which no one disputes, and not on whether Anglican worship is beautiful, which it often is.

response.heading: The break in orders: what Leo XIII actually decided.
response.body:
In Apostolicae Curae (13 September 1896), Pope Leo XIII declared Anglican ordinations “absolutely null and utterly void.” His judgment rested on two defects in the new Edwardine Ordinal drawn up after the break with Rome. First, a defect of form: the rite dropped the language of a sacrificing priesthood — the power to “consecrate and offer the true Body and Blood of Christ” — leaving a bare “Receive the Holy Ghost” that no longer expressed what the Catholic priesthood is.

Second, a defect of intention, read from the rite itself. The Ordinal was deliberately framed to express a different ministry: pastoral and preaching, not sacrificial. A sacrament requires the intention to do what the Church does; a rite designed to exclude the sacrificing priesthood cannot confer it, whatever the personal faith of the man ordained. Leo did not doubt that the first post-Reformation bishops had themselves been validly ordained before the break — the break came from the defective rite they then used to ordain their successors, so apostolic succession was lost in the transmission.

This was not a passing opinion, and it has not been walked back. In 1998 the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith listed Leo’s declaration among the truths “to be held definitively” — connected to revelation by historical necessity, though not themselves declared as divinely revealed. When Anglican clergy enter the Catholic Church today, they are ordained as Catholic priests absolutely, not conditionally: the Church judges their previous orders null, not merely doubtful.

response.heading: Why that means no Eucharist — and no intercommunion.
response.body:
No valid priesthood means no valid consecration, and that is the whole chain. Christ sent the apostles as He had been sent — “As the Father has sent me, so I send you,” breathing on them and giving them power to forgive sins (John 20:21-23) — and the apostles passed that ministry on by the laying on of hands, as Paul left Titus in Crete to “ordain priests throughout the communities” (Titus 1:5). Break the chain of ordination, and the Eucharist celebrated at the end of it is a memorial service, not the sacrifice of the Mass.

The Catechism says exactly this about Reformation communities. They “have not preserved the proper reality of the Eucharistic mystery in its fullness, especially because of the absence of the sacrament of Holy Orders,” and “it is for this reason that, for the Catholic Church, Eucharistic intercommunion with these communities is not possible” (CCC 1400). Sharing the Eucharist is not a courtesy between friendly churches; it declares a unity of faith, orders, and communion with Peter that does not yet exist, and to pretend otherwise would be a lie told at the altar.

The Orthodox contrast proves the rule rather than breaking it. The Eastern Churches kept apostolic succession and valid orders through their schism, so the Catechism says they “possess true sacraments, above all — by apostolic succession — the priesthood and the Eucharist” (CCC 1399). The difference is not favoritism: it is whether the chain survived. Where it survived, the sacraments are recognized; where the ordaining rite itself was emptied of the priesthood, they are not.

response.heading: The open door: the Personal Ordinariates.
response.body:
The Church’s answer to Anglicans is an invitation, not a closed door. With the apostolic constitution Anglicanorum Coetibus (4 November 2009), Pope Benedict XVI created Personal Ordinariates: structures equivalent to dioceses where Anglican communities entering full communion keep their liturgical and spiritual patrimony — the prayer-book tradition, the choral worship, the pastoral style — within the Catholic Church, rather than surrendering it.

Three ordinariates were erected in quick succession. Our Lady of Walsingham for England and Wales on 15 January 2011; the Chair of Saint Peter for the United States and Canada on 1 January 2012; and Our Lady of the Southern Cross for Australia on 15 June 2012. Their clergy, including married priests under the same pastoral exception first allowed in 1980, were ordained as Catholic priests and now celebrate a valid Eucharist in the Anglican tradition.

That is the shape of the Catholic hope for reunion. Jesus prayed “that they may all be one” (John 17:21) and promised “one sheepfold and one shepherd” (John 10:16). The ordinariates show what that unity looks like in practice: not absorption that erases what Anglicans love, but full communion that keeps it — because the goal was never to win an argument about orders, but to gather one flock around one altar.

simple: Anglicans are real Christians and their baptisms count, so we call them brothers. But in the 1500s the Church of England changed the ordination ceremony so it no longer made sacrificing priests — so the chain of real priests broke. Pope Leo XIII said in 1896 that Anglican ordinations are null and void, and the Church still holds that today. Without real priests there is no real Eucharist to share, which is why Catholics and Anglicans cannot take Communion together yet. The good news: since 2009, whole Anglican groups can join the Catholic Church together and keep their own style of worship, in the Personal Ordinariates.
oneLiner: Anglican baptisms are valid but their orders were judged null in 1896, so there is no valid Eucharist to share — and the Ordinariates are the way home.
